content: This report provides an update to the 2008 recommendations issued by the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) regarding the use of influenza vaccines for the prevention and control of seasonal influenza. It includes new and updated information for the 2009 influenza season. The 2009 recommendations emphasize the following key points: 1. Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all children aged 6 months to 18 years during the 2009-2010 influenza season. 2. Vaccines containing the 2009-2010 trivalent vaccine virus strains—A/Brisbane/59/2007 (H1N1)-like, A/Brisbane/10/2007 (H3N2)-like, and B/Brisbane/60/2008-like antigens—should be used. 3. Updated recommendations for influenza diagnosis and antiviral use will be published before the start of the 2009-2010 influenza season. Vaccination efforts should begin as soon as the vaccine becomes available and continue throughout the influenza season. The CDC's influenza website provides access to these recommendations and any updates or supplements that may be required during the 2009-2010 season. In the United States, annual seasonal influenza epidemics typically occur from late fall through early spring. Influenza viruses can infect individuals of all age groups, but infection rates are highest among children. Severe illness and death rates are highest among individuals aged over 65 years, children under 2 years, and those with medical conditions that increase their risk of complications from influenza. On average, approximately 36,000 deaths occurred annually during 1990-1999, and 226,000 hospitalizations occurred annually during 1979-2001 due to influenza epidemics. Annual influenza vaccination remains the most effective method for preventing influenza virus infection and its complications. Vaccination is recommended for all individuals aged 6 months and older who do not have contraindications to vaccination. Trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (TIV) can be administered to any individual aged 6 months and older, including those with high-risk conditions. Live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) may be used for healthy, non-pregnant individuals aged 2-49 years. However, individuals with underlying medical conditions that increase their risk for influenza complications should only receive TIV, as the safety and efficacy of LAIV in these populations have not been established. Children aged 6 months to 18 years should receive annual influenza vaccination. Vaccination efforts should prioritize children and adolescents at higher risk for influenza complications, including those aged 6 months to 4 years, those with chronic pulmonary, cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, neurologic, hematologic, or metabolic disorders, immunosuppressed individuals, those receiving long-term aspirin therapy, residents of long-term care facilities, and pregnant individuals during the influenza season. Children under 6 months of age cannot receive influenza vaccination, so vaccination of their caregivers and close contacts is critical. Antiviral medications serve as an adjunct to vaccination and are effective when used for treatment or chemoprophylaxis following exposure to influenza virus. However, the emergence of antiviral resistance among circulating strains has complicated treatment and prophylaxis recommendations. Updated antiviral treatment and chemoprophylaxis guidelines will be issued separately. In April 2009, a novel influenza A (H1N1) virus, antigenically distinct from human influenza A (H1N1) viruses circulating since 1977, was identified as the cause of a respiratory illness that spread globally. The symptoms of novel H1N1 infection are similar to those of seasonal influenza, and specific diagnostic testing is required to differentiate between the two. The epidemiology and prevention strategies for this novel virus are still under investigation, and further guidance will be published separately. The ACIP provides annual recommendations for the prevention and control of influenza. These recommendations are based on a review of influenza burden, vaccine effectiveness, safety, coverage, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and anticipated vaccine supply. The ACIP also considers data from published studies, vaccine and antiviral production updates, and input from state and local vaccination program representatives. Influenza A and B viruses cause epidemic human disease. Influenza A viruses are categorized into subtypes based on hemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface antigens. Since 1977, influenza A (H1N1), A (H3N2), and influenza B viruses have circulated globally. Influenza B viruses are not categorized into subtypes but are divided into two genetic lineages (Yamagata and Victoria). Immunity to surface antigens, particularly hemagglutinin, reduces the likelihood of infection. However, frequent antigenic drift necessitates annual reassessment of vaccine strains. Influenza-related complications requiring urgent medical care, including hospitalizations and deaths, can result from direct viral effects, ageor pregnancy-related complications, or exacerbation of underlying chronic diseases. Annual influenza epidemics in the United States have been associated with an estimated 55,000 to 431,000 hospitalizations and 17,000 to 51,000 deaths per epidemic. The risk of complications, hospitalizations, and deaths is highest among individuals aged over 65 years, young children, and those with high-risk medical conditions. Among children under 5 years, influenza-related illness is a common cause of medical visits. Hospitalization rates are highest among infants and young children and are similar to rates for other high-risk groups. Influenza-associated deaths are uncommon among children, but the majority occur in those without known high-risk conditions. Vaccination coverage remains low among many target groups, and strategies to improve coverage should be implemented. Hospitalization rates during influenza season are substantially increased for individuals aged over 65 years and those with underlying medical conditions. Influenza is a significant contributor to the annual increase in deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza during winter months. The risk of influenza-related death is highest among the oldest elderly individuals. The duration and severity of influenza symptoms are prolonged among individuals with HIV infection. Influenza vaccination is recommended for all adults without contraindications, particularly those at higher risk for complications or those in close contact with high-risk individuals.
